central_question: Why does a coffee cup stay hot even after the liquid is gone?
hook: A steaming mug sits on a counter, its surface still warm, yet the cup is empty. How can a dry cup feel hot?
aha_moment: The mug’s ceramic walls absorb and store a huge amount of heat from the coffee; their low thermal conductivity and high heat capacity make that heat leak out slowly, keeping the outer surface warm for minutes.

story_arc.reveal: A mug feels hot even though it’s empty
The mug itself is the heat source, not the coffee
We all feel a mug’s warmth after pouring out coffee

story_arc.purpose: First reveal – conduction into the mug
story_arc.reveal: Coffee at 80 °C pours into a room‑temperature ceramic mug; heat flows into the walls
The 200 g mug with 0.93 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ heat capacity stores ~12 kJ of energy

story_arc.purpose: Midpoint reversal – low conductivity creates a gradient
story_arc.reveal: Ceramic’s 1.5 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ conductivity means the inner wall stays hot while the outer cools slowly
Only a thin film of moisture evaporates, removing little heat; now loss is by convection and radiation
Convection dominates; radiation is <10 % of loss, so heat leaks out over minutes
The outer wall stays noticeably above room temperature for several minutes, giving the “hot” sensation
required_facts: Outer wall above ambient for minutes

story_arc.reveal: Eventually the stored energy is exhausted and the mug cools to room temperature

ending_payoff: So the next time you touch an empty mug, remember it’s the ceramic’s own thermal memory, not the coffee, that keeps it warm—turning a simple cup into a tiny, slow‑release heat bank.
